0.1 This

FOREWORD

Indian Standard was adopted by the Indian Standards Institution on 17 May 1982, after the draft finalized by the Metallic Finishes Sectional Committee had been approved by the Structural and Metals Division Council. 0.2 This recommended practice is included as an aid in establishing and maintaining a procedure for preparing zinc alloy die castings for electroplating. It is not intended as a standardized procedure and should be used merely as a guide. The sequence of the individual cycles and concentrations of various solutions are flexible and may be varied to fit the conditions of the individual plating department. The purpose of the cycles is to prepare the work to take a sound, adherent electroplated coating. 0.2.1 For the manufacture of zinc alloy die castings, ing to IS : 713-1981* may be chosen. 0.3 In derived Testing the preparation from ASTM B and Materials. material conform-

of this standard considerable assistance has been 252-1969 issued by the American Society for

3.2 Abrasives with a grit size of 53 to 75 pm mesh glued on cloth wheels or continuous cloth belts that run over flexible back-up wheels are usually used for mechanical polishing of parting lines. Wheel diameters range from 5 to 40 cm depending on the complexity of the shape. Wheels are rotated with a maximum peripheral speed of 2 500 m/min. A peripheral speed of 2 100 m/min should not to be exceeded with belts. Lower speeds of the order of 1 100 to 1400 m /min are fairly common for small die castings polished on small diameter wheels. Abrasive belts should not be used dry but should be lubricated with a small amount of grease. Die castings usually are handled individually to polish parting lines smooth. This may require 30 seconds or less for small castings, and sometimes 5 or 6 minutes for larger ones. 3.3 Tumbling in horizontal barrels, loaded with abrasive stones, such as limestone, preformed and fused aluminium oxide, ceramic shapes or abrasive-loaded plastic chips, and a lubricant such as soap or detergent solution, removes parting line burrs from die castings in 4 to 12 hours. The barrels may be rotated at 4 ppm. Higher speeds reduce the time cycles and costs, but also increase the danger of impingement of parts against zinc surface. A hexagonal barrel with a capacity of 0'5 ms may be loaded with 450 kg of abrasive stones of chips and 90 kg of zinc die castings. 3.4 Vibration in a bed of resin-bonded abrasive chips removes partingline burrs, typically in 1 to 4 hours. Frequencies range from 700 to 2 100 cycles per minute and amplitudes from 0.8 to 6.4 mm. A vibrating tub with a capacity of 0.5 ma may be loaded with about 900 kg of abrasive media and 180 kg of zinc die castings. A dilute solution of detergent or soap is continuously metered through the bed of media and parts to keep their surfaces clean and maximize surface smoothing. Parting lines may be mechanically polished before vibratory processing when a large amount of flash shall be removed. 4

c) Vibratory finishing. Fissures, skin bli\ters and other defects with a depth of 25 to 50 pm may usually be erased with these metal removal methods. Deeper defects are infrequent. 4.2 Mechanical polishing for smoothing rough or defective surfaces is similar to mechanical polishing by smoothing parting line areas ( see 3.2 ). Parting lines and rough or defective surfaces are frequently polished by the same operator. If polishing is mechanized to advance die castings attached to a conveyor through successive belts or wheels to polish different areas, a manual operation may be required later to complete the smoothing of parting lines if they are too curved. The finish ranges from 0.2 to 0.6 pm depending on the abrasive and the pressure. 4.3 Smoothing by spinning in abrasives is accomplished by attaching die ca,tings to spindles or drums rotated with a peripheral speed of about 600 m/min in a slurry of abrasive material such as ground corn cubs or nut shells mixed with a small amount of grease or other lubricant. Time usually ranges from 5 to 10 minutes and the finish from 0.1 to 0_2rm, depending on the abrasive. 4.4 Vibrating tubs loaded with plastic chips ( such as polyurethane ) impregnated with an abrasive ( such as, aluminium oxide ) smooth the surfaces of die castings in 2 to 4 hours when frequencies are in the range of 1 700 to 2 100 cycles per minute and amplitudes are adjusted to 3.2 to 6.4 mm. Vibratory machines produce a finish of 0.15 to 0.25 pm, with a cutting rate of 5 pm/h. A smoother finish of O-075 to 0.125 pm may be obtained with plastic media containing finer abrasive, which removes metal at a slower rate. Media and zinc parts are usually loaded witharatioof5: lor6: 1. Surface gouges may occur with a smaller ratio. 5. BUFFING castings are buffed to produce a mirror-like finish, suitable for plating with conventional solutions, when good levelling plating solutions are not available. Buffing may be omitted, however, for die castings which have good cast surfaces or which may be uniformly polished to a finish of 0'25 pm, if solutions with good levelling power are used for plating copper and nickel. 5

5.1 Die

IS : 10173 - 1902
5.2 Die castings are buffed on cloth wheels rotated at a peripheral speed not exceeding 2 150 m/min. Slower speeds, of the order of 1 100 to 1 600 mlmin are used for small die castings. Euffing compounds should be made with a binder that is readily emulsified or saponified during alkaline cleaning. The abrasive may be tripoli ( amorphous silica ) or lime, mixed with about 25 percent of tallow or other lubricants. Cornpounds suspended in a liquid are preferred for automatic buffing machines that advance die castings through a succession of buffs of varying diameter and width, which individually smooth different surface areas. Buffs are usually made of cloth with a thread count of 34 to 37/cm. A finish of 0.025 to 0.05 pm may be produced by buffing. The smoothing rate is influenced by the temperature of the metal surface ( faster at approximately 150�C than at lower temperatures ). 5.3 After buffing, surfaces may be cleaned by passing them over a relatively clean, dry wheel to remove buffing compound. This will reduce the demand placed on the precleaning solution. 6. PRECLEANING

AND

RINSING

6.1 It is strongly

recommended that the preliminary removal of most of the buffing compound and other soil in a precleaning operation be done as soon as possible after buffing and polishing. Most buffing compounds become substantially more difficult to remove after ageing several days. from zinc speaking, cleaning

6.2 There are several methods by which soils may be removed die castings prior to final alkaline electrocleaning. Generally these fall into three main classes : solvent degreasing, emulsion and cleaning with aqueous ba:e detergents.

6.2.1 Solvent Degreasing - Cold solvents, such as, mineral spirits, methylene chloride, trichloroethylene, perchloroethylene and tr:chlcroethane are used with brushing to loosen packed buffing compound but this method usually is not practical for mass production conditions. Simple dipping in cold solvent is often ineffective. Vapour degreasing with trichloroethylene or perchloroethylene is widely practiced. Cften the buffed die castings are sprayed with, or immersed in, hot solLent for This is followed by condenmechanical removal of heavy soil deposits. sation of hot, clean solvent vapours on the work; this removes the last The method is very effective, provided traces of grease and compound. adequate measures are taken to remove the very fine abrasive and metallic particles from the work. Cost of the chlorinated solvent is higher than wet cleaning methods, but this is often offset by lower equipment, floor Trichloroethylene and perchloroethylene space, and heat requirements. are nonflammable as used in vapour degreabing and, while relativ-ely safe as chlorinated solvents go, still shall be used in systems designed to 6

IS :10173

- 1982

Suppliers of chlorinated protect personnel from inhalation of vapours. solvents should be consulted as to the safety of a given installation. Not more than 100 ppm of either trichloroethylene or perchloroethylene are considered safe in the working atmosphere for a normal 8 hour working day. 6.2.2 Emulsion Cleaning
6.2.2.1 Packed buffing compound may be loosened, and to some extent removed, by immersion in various hydrocarbon-water emulsions. These emulsions are available in several forms, including unstable emulsions ( diphase cleaners ), invert type emulsions, mixtures of emulsions and alkaline cleaners, and stable emulsions. Such emulsion cleaners usually have a suitable hydrocarbon base, such as korosene or a higher flashpoint solvent to which are added emulsifiers, soaps, and inhibitors to pomt etching of the die castings. i

6.2.2.2 These emulsions normally are used hot, at about 804C, as a soak, sometimes with agitation, for about 2 to 5 minutes. Buffing compound not removed in the emulsion soak is sufficiently softened so that it is easily removed in an alkaline spray wash operation that normally follows. Its 6.2.2.3 Emulsion cleaning is effective and relatively low in cost. principal disadvantage is the danger of carryover of hydrocarbon solvent into plating baths because of incomplete rinsing. For this reason, it is very important that proper alkaline cleaning and thorough rinsing follow to ensure solvent removal from blind holes, defects in rack coatings, and recesses. 6.2.3 Aqueous Base Detergents - Hot mixtures of emulsifiers and wetting agents, sometimes combined with mild alkaline phosphates or borates, are used as presoaks to soften and remove buffing compound. Combining these soaks with ultrasonics is particularly effective on impacted buffing compound. Such detergent soaks are followed by spray cleaning with an alkaline cleaner or spray rinsing with warm water before electrocleaning. Sometimes conventional alkaline soak cleaners are used for precleaning die castings with little or no buffing compound on them. These alkaline cleaners should be mild and inhibited since strong alkali will attack the castings.
- Alkaline spray cleaners-z 6.3 Power Spray Alkaline Washing widely used, during the initial cleaning operation or following initial This is accomplished with presoaks in emulsions, solvents, or detergents. conveyrized units, equipped with washing, draining, rinsing, and draining sections. The solution, heated to about 8O'C, is sprayed with a pressure of 170 to 205 kPa through nozzels on 20 to 30 cm centres in the washing area. A typical solution may contain 10 g/l of mixed alkalis, such as, 7

ALKALINE ELECTROCLEANING AND RINSING

7.1 Electrocleaning is necessary for completing the removal of oil, grease, and soil, and to ensure good electroplate adhesion. Anodic cleaning is usually selected for zinc alloys in preference to cathodic cleaning. Anodic current densities usually range from about l-6 to 3.2 A/dm'. Time cycles vary from 25 to 45 seconds. 7.2 A typical solution for anodic cleaning contains 30 to 40 g/l of mixed alkalis such as trisodium phosphate and sodium metasilicate, 0.5 g/l of surfactant, and not more than 0.5 g/l of sodium hydroxide and is heated to 70 to 82�C. Lower temperatures may be required if time cycles shall be prolonged for more than 45 seconds, or if the transfer time from the electrocleaner to the first rinse is more than about 30 seconds. Operating an anodic electrocleaner at too dilute concentrations may over-etch the castings. 7.3 A thorough rinsing after electrocleaning is a must. A cycle including a warm water rinse, a cold water rinse, and a water spray rinse is recomThe rinses should be agitated mended after alkaline electrocleaning. the concentration of alkaline with air to dilute, as much as possible, and other surface indentations and solution in blind holes, grooves, Alkaline solution entrapped in surface crevices and pores will cavities. become sites for process blisters if alkaline cleaner concentrations are not reduced to very low levels by agitated cold water rinsing. Rinse water containing a high concentration of dissolved minerals should be avoided. 8. ACID

DIPPING

AND

RINSING

However, a solution containing 0.25 to 1 percent of sulphuric acid is frequently adopted for time cycles of 25 to 45 Stronger solutions will require more thorough rinsing after seconds. viscous acid solutions should be acid dipping. Highly concentrated, avoided. 8.2 The acid dip should remove all traces of black films or loosely adherent smut. For die castings prone to smut, including alloys containing more than about 0.25 percent copper, the acid solution may be ultrasonically agitated; this effectively prevents the formation of smut. 8

9. COPPER

STRIKING

9.1 A copper strike applied in a cyanide copper solution is normally the first plating step for all die castings to be electroplated with nickel and chromium. The thickness of the strike should be at least 1.0 pm for die castings that may be subsequently plated with bright copper in hightemperature cyanide solutions and at least 5.0'pm for die castings that may be plated with nickel after copper striking. A thickness of 3.0 to 4-O pm is recommended for die castings that may be subsequently electroplated with bright, levelling copper in copper sulphate-sulphuric acid solutions.
9.2 Solutions containing 20 to 45 g/l of copper cyanide, 10 to 20 g/l of free sodium cyanide, and 15 to 75 g/l of sodium carbonate are customary for strike solutions. However, copper striking solution based on potassium gives better covering to the zinc die cast surface, and the chances of appearing black spots in subsequent nickel-plating are minimized.

,

9.2.1 A few formulations include the molar equivalents of potassium cyanide in place of sodium cyanide. Other contain 15 to 35 g/l of Rochelle salt and or 3.8 to 7.5 g/l of sodium hydroxide in addition to the majl r constituents. Higher concentration of sodium hydroxide should be avoided to eliminate the attack on the basis netal. 3n many of the formulations use is made of addition agents, which reduce hexavalent chromium, facilitate in anode corrosion, and refine the grain structure. Cathode current densities normally range from 2.7 to 6.5 A/dma and solution temperatures from 50 to 57`C. Cyanic'e solutions ccntaining a higher concentration of copper cyanide and operated at a higher temperature should be avoided because of the danger of blister formation. The current should be on when work enters the copper striking solution.
9.3 The average cathode current density shall be balanced with the free sodium cyanide and the temperature of the solution to prevent burn'ng at edges and other high-current-density areas. W th an average cathoce current density of 2.7 A/c'm 4, the cathode current efficiency varies from A high terrperature, a high copper 30 to 60 percent for strike plating. cyanide concentration, and a low free cyanide concentration, within the limits given in 9.2, favour high efficiency. Ultrasonic agitation has been proposed for increasing cathode efficiency, the covering power in recessed areas, and improving the density of the copper deposit. Ultrasonic 9

IS:10173-1982
in cyanide-free

agitation has been reported as an important condition for copper striking solutions prepared with potassium pyrophosphate, copper pyrophosphate and potassium citrate, prior to bright copper piating in acid sulphate solutions.

9.4 High-purity copper anodes preferably oxygen free ( see IS : 2603Solutions 1964* ) are recommended for copper cyanide strike solutions. should be continuously filtered to avoid the inclusion of small particles that nucleate nodules during subsequent plating operations.
